Join the tables on order_id to create a single order-level DataFrame¶

Task:

  • Perform inner joins on order_id so that only orders present in all tables remain.
  • Join order tables in this order:
    1. df_orders with df_order_items
    2. result with df_shipping
    3. result with df_payments
  • Store the final DataFrame as df_orders_full.
  • Display head() and shape for df_orders_full.
In [ ]:
# Join the tables sequentially
df_final = pd.merge(df_orders, df_order_items, on='order_id', how = 'inner')
df_final = pd.merge(df_final, df_shipping, on='order_id', how = 'inner')
df_final = pd.merge(df_final, df_payments, on='order_id', how = 'inner')
df_orders_full = df_final

1.1 Data Loading and Joining Summary¶

We loaded four separate relational tables ('orders', 'order_item', 'shipping', 'payments') and merged them sequentially using an inner join on the unique 'order_id'. By linking these relational tables, we created a comprehensive view of the unified dataset of the transaction records, functioning as the foundation for analyzing the end to end customer journey.

1.2 Data Cleaning (3 marks)¶

We now clean df_orders_full so it is ready for analysis.

Handle missing values¶

Task:

  • For numerical columns: replace missing values with the median of that column.
  • For categorical columns: replace missing values with the mode (most frequent value).
  • Drop any rows where order_id or payment_type is missing (if any remain)

Work directly on df_orders_full.

In [ ]:
# Separate columns by data type for appropriate data imputation
numerical_cols = df_orders_full.select_dtypes(include=['number']).columns
categorical_cols = df_orders_full.select_dtypes(include=['object']).columns

# Fill missing numerical values with the median
df_orders_full[numerical_cols] = df_orders_full[numerical_cols].fillna(df_orders_full[numerical_cols].median())

# Fill missing categorical values with the mode (most frequent value)
for col in categorical_cols:
    col_mode = df_orders_full[col].mode()
    if not df_orders_full[col].mode().empty:
        df_orders_full[col] = df_orders_full[col].fillna(col_mode[0])

# Drop records lacking tracking IDs as they cannot be tied to a customer
df_orders_full.dropna(subset=['order_id', 'payment_type'], inplace=True)

Remove clearly invalid numeric records¶

Task:

  • Remove rows where:
    • num_items ≤ 0, or
    • order_total_value ≤ 0, or
    • total_item_price < 0, or
    • total_freight_value < 0.
In [ ]:
# Filter out logically impossible entries

df_orders_full = df_orders_full[
    (df_orders_full['num_items'] > 0) &
    (df_orders_full['order_total_value'] > 0) &
    (df_orders_full['total_item_price'] >= 0) &
    (df_orders_full['total_freight_value'] >= 0)]

1.2 Data Cleaning Summary¶

In the process of data clearning, we imputed missing numerical values with the median and missing categorical values with mode. We also performed rows dropping for the rows missing critical key identifies and performed filtering out for these logically invalid numeric records. This is because "dirty" data leads to incorrect business decisions. Missing categories skew product trend analysis, and negative prices heavily distort revenue and profitability analysis. Replacing missing values and filtering out invalid records guarantees that strategic decisions and financial insight are based on reliable, high-quality data.

1.3 Data Transformation (3 marks)¶

Next, we perform sanity checks and create new features that will be useful later.

Sanity checks on counts and values¶

Task:

  • Keep only rows where both:
    • num_items ≥ num_unique_products,
    • order_total_value ≥ total_item_price + total_freight_value
In [ ]:
# Sanity Logic Checks: total items must be greater or equal to unique products; total order value should cover the price of items plus shipping freight
df_orders_full = df_orders_full[
    (df_orders_full['num_items'] >= df_orders_full['num_unique_products']) &
    (df_orders_full['order_total_value'] >= (df_orders_full['total_item_price'] + df_orders_full['total_freight_value']))]

df_orders_full.shape

(46287, 15)

Create order_value_per_item¶

Task:

  • Create a new column order_value_per_item defined as total_item_price / num_items.
In [ ]:
# Calculate average value per item for the order
df_orders_full['order_value_per_item'] = df_orders_full['total_item_price'] / df_orders_full['num_items']

Create order_size_category¶

Task:

  • Create a new categorical column order_size_category with values:
    • "Small" if num_items ≤ 2
    • "Medium" if num_items ≤ 5
    • "Large" if num_items > 5
In [ ]:
# Group orders into analyzable segements: small, medium, large
df_orders_full['order_size_category'] = pd.cut(df_orders_full['num_items'], bins = [0, 2, 5, np.inf], labels = ['Small', 'Medium', 'Large'])

1.3 Data Transformation Summary¶

We apllied sanity check ensuring the logic between aggregate and individual metrics hold up. And we engineered new features with including average cost of items and order size category by item count. Creating the order_value_per_item metric acts as a proxy for the price segment of the order. Transforming raw data into segmented categories allows for deeper behavioral analysis.

Furthermore, categorizing orders into "Small", "Medium", and "Large" sizes clusters customers by purchasing behavior. This clustering helps identify distinct order segments for targeted promotions and optimized fulfillment strategies.

We implement an 80/20 train-test split (37,029 training, 9,258 test orders) to balance learning data with unbiased evaluation. The test set simulates production reality where the payment system encounters new orders daily. Setting random_state=RANDOM_STATE ensures reproducibility across team members and enables consistent model comparisons. This foundation supports trustworthy A/B testing when deploying model updates.

TODO: Briefly explain the importance of using a test dataset.

Using a test dataset is crucial because it allows us to evaluate how well a machine learning model generalizes to new, unseen data. If we only evaluate a model on the data it was trained on, we risk 'overfitting,' where the model memorizes the training data rather than learning the underlying patterns.

We employ Label Encoding over One-Hot to avoid dimensionality explosion (50 states + 71 categories = 121+ columns). High dimensionality causes sparse features, excessive computational cost, and overfitting risk. Our strategy handles unseen categories (new products, states post-training) by assigning distinct labels, preventing production crashes. Note: order_id risks overfitting and should be removed in production deployment.

TODO: Briefly explain why categorical encoding is required for machine learning models.

Categorical encoding is required for machine learning models because most algorithms are designed to work with numerical input data. Categorical variables, which represent distinct groups or categories (e.g., 'shipped', 'delivered'), cannot be directly processed by these mathematical models. Encoding converts these categories into a numerical format that the models can understand and incorporate into their calculations, allowing them to learn relationships and make predictions based on these features.

Scaling ensures all features contribute equally to distance-based algorithms like Logistic Regression and SVM. Without scaling, features with large ranges (e.g., order_total_value) dominate gradient descent, causing slow convergence and suboptimal performance. We fit the scaler on training data only to prevent data leakage from test set. This preprocessing step is critical for models sensitive to feature magnitude.

TODO: Briefly explain why feature scaling is important for some classification models.

Because many machine learning algorithms are sensitive to the scale and magnitude of input features. Models like Logistic Regression rely on distance calculations or gradient descent optimization, which can be heavily influenced by features with larger numerical ranges. Without scaling, features with wider ranges might dominate the distance calculations or gradient updates, leading to suboptimal model performance, slower convergence, or inaccurate results.

Scaling ensures that all features contribute equally to the model's learning process, helping these algorithms perform more effectively and efficiently.

# TODO: Compute evaluation metrics for all three models

def evaluate_model(y_true, y_pred, model_name):
    accuracy = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
    precision = precision_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted')
    recall = recall_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted')
    f1 = f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted')

    return {
        'Model': model_name,
        'Accuracy': accuracy,
        'Precision': precision,
        'Recall': recall,
        'F1-Score': f1
    }

The confusion matrices reveal that Logistic Regression and SVM focus on majority classes, achieving high accuracy but poor minority coverage. Decision Tree attempts broader classification but suffers from noise and variance. Random Forest successfully balances accuracy with F1-Score, demonstrating superior minority class handling. These visualizations confirm that ensemble methods provide the most robust solution for imbalanced payment type prediction.

TODO: Briefly comment on the strengths and weaknesses of each model, and any impact of class imbalance handling.

Logistic Regression¶

  • Strengths: Achieved high accuracy by playing it "safe" -- it correctly identified the majority class (0) very well.

  • Weaknesses: The model have almost zero predictive power for minority classes 1, 2, and 3. It is essentially acting as binary classifiers for classes 0 and 4, which makes them unsuitable if detecting the minority classes is important.

SVM¶

  • Strengths: Same as logistic regression, achieved high accuracy by correctly identified the majority class (0) very well.

  • Weaknesses: Worst model in this task. Simply classified everything as 1, and the training time was significantly longer (104s) than other models.

Decision Tree¶

  • Strengths: It is the only model that attempts to classify the minority classes (1 and 3) with some frequency. Trained very fast, only 2 seconds (although might that be a disatvantage?).

  • Weaknesses: It is very "noisy." While it tries to predict more classes, it gets them wrong often, leading to the lowest accuracy and a mediocre F1-score.

Random Forest¶

  • Strengths: This is our strongest model. It maintains the high accuracy of the linear models while significantly improving the F1-Score. It is better at distinguishing between class 0 and class 4 and makes a decent attempt at class 3.

  • Weaknesses: Even with its ensemble power, it still fails to identify classes 1 and 2 effectively.

Final Recommendation¶

TODO: Select and justify your choice of the best model.

Selected Model: Random Forest

Justification based on:

  1. Evaluation Metrics:

    Random Forest outperformed all other models across every key metric. It achieved the highest Accuracy (62.79%) and the highest F1-Score (0.5776). While Logistic Regression and SVM had comparable accuracy, their lower F1-scores reveal that they were largely ignoring minority classes, whereas Random Forest maintained a better balance between Precision and Recall.

  2. Class Imbalance Considerations:

    The dataset is heavily imbalanced toward Class 0. While Logistic Regression and SVM "cheated" by primarily predicting the majority classes, Random Forest showed the best ability to correctly classify samples in Class 3 and Class 4. It demonstrated superior resilience to the noise and scarcity of the minority class data.

  3. Model Complexity and Interpretability:

    As an ensemble of Decision Trees, Random Forest reduces the high variance (overfitting) seen in the single Decision Tree model. While it is more complex than Logistic Regression, it provides valuable "Feature Importance" scores, which allow us to understand which variables are driving the classifications—a critical factor for business or scientific applications.

  4. Practical Deployment Considerations:

    Random Forest is highly "parallelizable," meaning it can be trained quickly on multi-core processors. It also requires less data pre-processing (like scaling or normalization) compared to SVM and Logistic Regression, making the deployment pipeline simpler and less prone to errors when new data is introduced.

Why this model is preferred over others:

Logistic Regression and SVM failed to provide any utility for the minority classes (1, 2, and 3), rendering them ineffective for a multi-class problem. The single Decision Tree was too erratic and lacked the predictive power needed. Random Forest is the only model that successfully captured the underlying patterns of the data while maintaining the highest overall performance ceiling.

Model Explainability/Interpretability¶

TODO: Comment on the explainability/interpretability of each model.

Logistic Regression:

This is one of the most transparent models. Because it is a linear model, each feature is assigned a coefficient. You can directly see how a change in an input variable affects the probability of a class (log-odds).

Decision Tree:

Decision trees are highly interpretable because they mimic human logic through a series of if-then-else splits. You can literally print a flowchart of the model to see exactly which feature thresholds lead to which classification. However, if the tree is very deep (to handle the class imbalance you have), it can become a "comb" that is harder to read.

SVM:

SVMs are notoriously difficult to interpret, particularly when using non-linear kernels (like RBF). They transform data into a high-dimensional space to find a separating hyperplane. While you can identify "Support Vectors" (the most critical data points), you cannot easily explain the relationship between a single input feature and the final output in a way that makes sense to a non-technical audience.

Random Forest:

While a single tree is easy to read, a "forest" of hundreds of trees is much harder to visualize. We can’t easily trace the logic of the entire ensemble at once. However, we gain interpretability through Feature Importance rankings, which tell us which variables had the biggest impact on the overall predictions across the entire forest.

Conclusion¶

Summarize your findings and key takeaways from this assignment.

Findings and Key Takeaways from Assignment 2:¶

  1. Data Preprocessing is Crucial:

    • Categorical Encoding: Converting categorical features (like order_id, order_status, top_product_category, customer_state, order_size_category) into numerical representations was essential because most machine learning algorithms cannot directly process text-based data. Label Encoding, as applied, allowed models to interpret these features, although care was taken to handle unseen categories in the test set to maintain consistency.
    • Numerical Scaling: Scaling numerical features using StandardScaler (e.g., order_total_value, num_items, avg_item_price) was vital. Algorithms sensitive to feature magnitudes, such as Logistic Regression and SVM, perform better when all features are on a similar scale, preventing features with larger ranges from dominating the learning process. This leads to faster convergence and improved model performance.

  2. Comprehensive Model Evaluation is Necessary:

    • Relying solely on Accuracy can be misleading, especially with imbalanced datasets. Our dataset, where credit_card was the majority payment_type, showed that models like Logistic Regression and SVM could achieve relatively high accuracy by simply predicting the majority class, but failed to identify minority classes.
    • Precision, Recall, and F1-Score were critical for a nuanced understanding of model performance. The F1-Score, in particular, provided a balanced measure that accounted for both false positives and false negatives, highlighting that models like Random Forest, despite slightly lower accuracy than some, had a much better overall predictive capability across all classes.
    • Confusion Matrices offered a visual breakdown of predictions, clearly illustrating where models excelled or struggled with specific payment types, thereby exposing the limitations of models that predominantly predicted the majority class.

  3. Trade-offs in Model Complexity, Interpretability, and Performance:

    • Logistic Regression: Simple, highly interpretable, and computationally efficient. However, its linear nature struggled with the complex relationships in the data, especially with class imbalance, resulting in poor performance on minority classes.
    • Decision Tree: Generally interpretable (though deep trees can be complex) and fast to train. While it attempted to classify more diverse payment types, it suffered from high variance, leading to the lowest overall performance.
    • SVM: Offers strong generalization with non-linear relationships but is computationally intensive and very difficult to interpret. In our case, the chosen SVM model showed severe limitations in handling class imbalance, effectively predicting only one class, making it unsuitable.
    • Random Forest: An ensemble method that trades off some interpretability for significantly improved performance and robustness against overfitting. It performed the best overall, balancing complexity with predictive power.

Assignment 1's cleaning (99,441→46,287 orders) removed minority payment types, creating imbalance in Assignment 2. Assignment 3's clustering (5 segments) and association rules (furniture_decor 5.3x in large orders) offer feature engineering opportunities. Adding customer_segment features could improve payment prediction by encoding behavioral patterns.

For production, deploy Random Forest (F1: 0.5776) with data drift monitoring and SMOTE for class imbalance. Future improvements: leverage clustering features, tune hyperparameters, remove order_id, investigate temporal payment patterns.

Task: Unsupervised Learning¶

1: Data Preprocessing for Unsupervised Learning [1 Mark]¶

1.1 Create all_orders_df (one row per order)¶

Create a new DataFrame called all_orders_df with the following columns:

Identifier:

  • order_id — Unique identifier of the order
  • basket_size — Monetary value of the order (from order_total_value)
  • basket_qty — Number of items in the order (from num_items)
  • freight_ratio — Proportion of the order value that is freight (computed as total_freight_value / order_total_value)

  • top_product_category — The dominant product category in the order
  • payment_type — The payment method used
  • order_size_category — The order size category (Small/Medium/Large)

2: Determine the Optimal Number of Clusters [3 Marks]¶

2.1 Run K-Means for Different Cluster Numbers¶

  • Use only the four numerical features from orders_analysis_df (basket_size, basket_qty, freight_ratio, product_diversity) for clustering.
  • Run K-means clustering from k = 3 to 9 clusters.
  • Important: First scale the numerical features using StandardScaler before fitting K-means.
  • In each run, calculate the inertia of the cluster and store the values for each k (3 to 9) in a list or table.

Inertia is a measure of how tightly packed the clusters are. It is the sum of squared distances between each point and its assigned cluster center (centroid). Lower inertia indicates that the clusters are more compact, and the points are closer to their centroids, suggesting better clustering.

In [15]:
# 2.1 ANSWER: Run K-means for k=3 to 9 and calculate inertia
X = orders_analysis_df[[
    "basket_size",
    "basket_qty",
    "freight_ratio",
    "product_diversity"
]]

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)

inertia_values = []
for k in range(3, 10):
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=37)
    kmeans.fit(X_scaled)
    inertia_values.append(kmeans.inertia_)

list(zip(range(3,10), inertia_values))

2.2 Elbow Method for Optimal Clusters¶

  • Plot the inertia (y-axis) against the number of clusters (x-axis) to identify the optimal number of clusters using the Elbow method.

The Elbow Method helps in selecting the number of clusters by identifying where the inertia starts to decrease more slowly.

To finalize our segmentation strategy, we visualize the relationship between the number of clusters and the Inertia (the sum of squared distances within each cluster). This allows us to pinpoint the elbow point where adding more clusters provides diminishing returns in explaining the variance of our data.

Based on the Elbow plot above, the optimal number of clusters is k = 5. The inertia drops sharply from k = 3 to 5, and after k = 5, the rate of decrease slows down significantly, indicating diminishing returns. Therefore, k = 5 is the possible elbow point where the trade-off between model complexity and cluster cohesion is optimal.

4: Market Basket Analysis (Association Rule Mining) [8 Marks]¶

4.1 Context: What is Market Basket Analysis?¶

Market Basket Analysis is an unsupervised learning technique that identifies which products, categories, or attributes are frequently observed together. In e-commerce, this helps answer questions such as:

  • "Which payment methods are preferred for which product categories?"
  • "Do certain order sizes correlate with specific product types?"
  • "What are the multi-dimensional patterns across category, payment, and order size?"

Association rules are commonly described using three key metrics:

  • Support: How frequently a pattern occurs (0-1 scale)
  • Confidence: Likelihood of the consequent given the antecedent (0-1 scale)
  • Lift: How much more likely the rule is compared to random chance (> 1 indicates a positive association)

The Apriori algorithm discovers frequent itemsets and then generates association rules from them.

In this task, you will perform Market Basket Analysis using the categorical features from all_orders_df to discover multi-dimensional associations between product category, payment type, and order size category.

4.2 Prepare Transaction Data [1 Mark]¶

Convert each order in all_orders_df into a simple "basket" representation.

Create a Python list called transactions, where each element represents one order and contains exactly three string items constructed from that order:

  • cat_{top_product_category} (e.g., cat_electronics, cat_furniture_decor)
  • pay_{payment_type} (e.g., pay_credit_card, pay_boleto)
  • size_{order_size_category} (e.g., size_Small, size_Large)

After constructing transactions, display the first 5 transactions to verify the format.

4.3 Encode Transactions and Apply Apriori Algorithm [2 Marks]¶

Use the mlxtend library to discover frequent itemsets and generate association rules.

  • Step 1: Encode transactions using TransactionEncoder and display the shape of the encoded DataFrame.
  • Step 2: Apply apriori() with min_support = 0.01 and use_colnames = True, then display the number of frequent itemsets found.
  • Step 3: Generate association rules using association_rules() with metric = 'lift' and min_threshold = 1.0, then display the number of rules generated.
In [33]:
# 4.3 ANSWER: Step 1 - Encode transactions
te = TransactionEncoder()
te_ary = te.fit(transactions).transform(transactions)
encoded_df = pd.DataFrame(te_ary, columns=te.columns_)
encoded_df.shape
Out[33]:
(46287, 79)

The TransactionEncoder converts list of category items into a one hot encoded binary format, which is the required mathematical structure for the Apriori algorithm to identify frequent patterns. The resulting encoded_df allows us to mathematically calculate degree across thousands of transactions simultaneously. Lastly, Checking the shape of the encoded data ensures we have successfully captured all unique attributes without losing any transaction records.

In [37]:
# 4.3 ANSWER: Step 2 - Apply Apriori
frequent_itemsets = apriori(
    encoded_df,
    min_support=0.01,
    use_colnames=True
)
print("Number of frequent itemsets:", frequent_itemsets.shape[0])

Number of frequent itemsets: 102

This step is the beginning of the pattern discovery phase using the Apriori Algorithm. By setting a minimum support threshold, we are filtering out rare or accidental combinations to focus on the significant shopping patterns that represent a meaningful portion of our business. Here we are filtering for patterns that appear in at least 1% of all orders. This ensures that the insights we generate are based on a statistically significant volume of customers. The number of frequent itemsets returned tells us how interconnected our categories, payment types, and order sizes are. A high count suggests a rich environment for cross-selling and targeted promotions.

In [38]:
# 4.3 ANSWER: Step 3 - Generate association rules
rules = association_rules(
    frequent_itemsets,
    metric="lift",
    min_threshold=1.0
)

print("Number of rules:", rules.shape[0])

Number of rules: 138

By applying the association_rules function, we move beyond simple frequency to understand the predictive power of our data. We use the Lift metric to identify relationships that are more than just coincidental, focusing on patterns where attributes are significantly more likely to occur together than if they were independent. A lift greater than 1.0 indicates a positive association, meaning the two attributes appear together more often than expected by chance.

This final step focuses on Insight Extraction. By isolating the top 10 rules based on lift, we are filtering out the noise to find the most significant and non-random correlations in our data. While Support tells us how common a pattern is, and Confidence tells us how reliable it is. Lift identifies the strongest relationships where the presence of one attribute truly drives the likelihood of the other. Despite being the smallest segment in volume, these high-value orders boast a 1.93 basket size and 1.82 quantity. Retention and loyalty programs are paramount here. With a 1.82 freight ratio, these customers are paying high shipping relative to their order value. This segment is a prime candidate for Free Shipping policy thresholds to increase their basket size. Low diversity indicates repeat purchases of identical items. Wholesale marketing would resonate well with this group.

4.5 Interpretation (3-4 sentences) [3 Marks]¶

Write a brief interpretation explaining:

  • What the top 3 unique rules tell you about customer behavior
  • Which combinations are most strongly associated (highest lift)
  • Why these associations might exist (business intuition)
  • Change the min_support value to 0.005 and 0.3 and comment on any changes in the rules identified

4.5 ANSWER:

The top 3 rules indicate that customers purchasing furniture_decor are highly likely to place Large number of orders. Conversely, customers buying bed_bath_table items are frequently associated with Medium-sized orders and tend to use credit cards for these transactions. The combination with the highest lift is (cat_furniture_decor) and (size_Large), with a lift value of 5.328. This suggests a very strong dependency, meaning these two occur together over five times more often than expected by chance. This association likely exists because furniture and decor are often purchased in sets to complete a room's look, leading to a high item count. Changing min_support to 0.005 will lower the threshold and increase the number of identified rules. This allows the model to capture niche patterns or infrequent combinations that may still have high business value or high lift. If min_support changes to 0.3, it will raise the threshold to 30%. In a diverse e-commerce dataset, it is rare for a specific combination of category, size, and payment type to occur in more than 30% of all total orders.

4.6 Business Recommendations (2-3 bullet points) [1 Mark]¶

Based on the discovered associations, provide actionable business recommendations for an e-commerce firm.

4.6 ANSWER:

[Write your business recommendations here as bullet points]

-Since furniture_decor is strongly associated with Large orders with a lift of 5.328, the business should offer bundles. By packaging complementary decor items as a single click-to-buy set, we can capitalize on the customer's tendency to buy multiple items at once in this category.

-The data shows a frequent association between bed_bath_table, Medium order sizes, and credit card payments. We should partner with banks to offer targeted cashback or reward points specifically for the this category of goods to increase the conversion rate of these mid-sized routine purchases.

-Introduce discounts for small and medium categories to incentivize customers to add more items, shifting orders toward the large category to improve shipping unit economics.

Tips¶

  • Rules with lift > 1.5 are considered strong associations; rules with lift > 2.0 are very strong.
  • When writing interpretations, explain not just the statistical strength but also the business logic behind the patterns.
